summary: Describes DICT, a query and response protocol over TCP that lets a client look up definitions in dictionary databases of natural languages. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It is a way for a program to ask a server what a word means, like opening a dictionary over the network.

questions: how to look up dictionary definitions over a network
what search strategies does dict support
subtitle: A protocol for client-server dictionary lookups over TCP.

tldr.problem: Freely available dictionaries existed but lacked a uniform interface, so they were difficult to access from a single location despite being potentially useful when combined.
tldr.mechanism: DICT is a TCP-based protocol where clients send commands to servers to look up word definitions, search using strategies like prefix matching, and retrieve metadata about available databases.
tldr.outcome: Clients can now query multiple dictionary databases through a standard interface, finding definitions from diverse sources without needing separate tools for each dictionary.

today: RFC 2229 is an Informational RFC defining the DICT protocol. It has not been obsoleted and remains the standard specification for dictionary server protocol implementations.

sections.title: What DICT Solves
sections.content:
For years, the Internet had a protocol called webster for accessing single dictionaries, but it declined in use. Meanwhile, freely available dictionaries like the Jargon File, WordNet, and the 1913 Webster's dictionary became public, yet each was scattered and lacked a uniform way to access them. DICT was designed to solve this: a TCP-based protocol that lets clients retrieve definitions from multiple dictionary databases through a single standardized interface.

Unlike webster, which works with one database at a time, DICT lets you search across multiple databases simultaneously, search using different strategies (like exact matching or prefix matching), and get information about the server itself.
sections.eli5: Before DICT, getting a definition from different dictionaries meant using different tools. DICT makes it so one tool can ask many different dictionaries the same way.

sections.title: Commands and Responses
sections.content:
DICT uses simple text-based commands sent over TCP port 2628. Commands are not case-sensitive and must fit on a single line (at most 1024 characters, or 6144 octets for UTF-8 encoding). Responses from the server use three-digit numeric codes similar to FTP and SMTP, where the first digit indicates success (2), failure (5), or intermediate state (1 or 3).

Text responses (like definition bodies) are sent as multiple lines, each ending with a carriage return and line feed, and terminated by a line containing only a period. If the original text contains a period as the first character, it is doubled so the client can distinguish it from the end marker.
sections.eli5: You type a command like 'look up this word', the server answers with a number like '250' (good) or '552' (not found), and if there is text, it sends the words line by line, ending with just a dot.

sections.title: Core Operations
sections.content:
The DEFINE command looks up a word in a specified database and returns its definition. The MATCH command finds words matching a pattern using a search strategy like 'exact' (exact match), 'prefix' (beginning of word), 'substring', or 'soundex' (for spelling correction). Special database names like '*' (search all databases) and '!' (search until found) allow broad queries.

The SHOW commands let you discover what the server offers: SHOW DB lists available databases, SHOW STRAT lists supported search strategies, SHOW INFO displays copyright and licensing information for a database, and SHOW SERVER shows administrative information. Clients can also send a CLIENT command to identify themselves, check server status with STATUS, or request HELP.
sections.eli5: DEFINE asks 'what does this word mean?', MATCH asks 'find me words that start with this', and SHOW commands ask 'what do you have available?'

sections.title: Authentication and Extensions
sections.content:
DICT includes optional authentication via the AUTH command, using MD5 checksums computed from a server-supplied message ID and a shared secret, similar to APOP in email. The server can indicate support for features in its welcome banner, such as 'mime' for MIME headers, 'auth' for authentication, or 'kerberos_v4' for Kerberos support. A SASLAUTH command is reserved for future Simple Authentication and Security Layer mechanisms.

The protocol was designed to be extensible: single-letter commands are reserved for debugging, and commands beginning with 'X' are reserved for experimental extensions. Virtual databases are permitted as an implementation detail to allow servers to group related databases without changing the protocol.
sections.eli5: To prevent unauthorized access to private dictionaries, servers can ask you to prove who you are with a secret password. New features can be added without breaking old servers.

sections.title: Sample Protocol Exchanges
sections.content:
When a client connects, the server sends code 220 with its name, version, and a unique message ID. The client can then send commands. For example, a HELP command returns code 113 followed by help text. A DEFINE command returns code 150 (definitions retrieved) followed by code 151 for each definition found, with the word, database name, and definition text, then code 250 when done. A SHOW DB command returns code 110 listing databases, terminated by a single period, then code 250.

If a lookup fails, the server returns code 552 (no match). The protocol supports pipelining: clients can send multiple commands at once and the server will process them in order. Timing information may be included in responses for debugging and performance analysis.
sections.eli5: The server greets you, you ask questions, it gives you answers with a number that tells you if it worked, and you can ask several questions without waiting for answers.
